The journey of Rabban Bar Sauma, a Christian monk born in Khanbaliq (Beijing), to the courts of Europe in 1287 and 1288 as the envoy of the Mongol Ilkhanate in Persia. It was the reverse of Marco Polo's travels.

Bar Sauma belonged to the Church of the East, the Syriac church that had spread across Asia. Around 1275 he set out from the Yuan lands of Kublai Khan on pilgrimage to Jerusalem with his pupil Markos. Wars stopped them in Persia, where Markos was made head of the church.

The Ilkhan Arghun wanted Christian allies against the Mamluks of Egypt, so he sent Bar Sauma west. He saw Constantinople, reached Rome while the papacy was vacant, met Philip IV of France in Paris and Edward I of England in Gascony, and was received by the new Pope Nicholas IV in 1288. He was welcomed everywhere, but no joint crusade followed. His account, in Syriac, survives.
